name: long120
truth:
Octopuses have three hearts. Two pump blood through the gills, and the third sends it to the rest of the body. Their blood is blue because it uses hemocyanin, a copper-based protein that carries oxygen efficiently in cold, low-oxygen seawater. This chemistry helps many species survive in deep, chilly habitats where oxygen is scarce.

Roughly two-thirds of an octopus's neurons sit in its arms rather than its central brain. This distributed system lets each arm taste, touch, and make some movement decisions without waiting for instructions from the brain. Researchers have observed severed arms continuing to grope for food. The nervous system therefore works more like a network of semi-independent controllers than a single command center.

Octopuses change color and texture within a fraction of a second. Thousands of chromatophores, small pigment sacs, are stretched open by muscles that the nervous system controls directly. Beneath them, iridophores and leucophores reflect light to create shimmering or white tones. Together these structures let an octopus blend into coral, sand, or rock almost instantly, and they also serve as signals to rivals and mates.

When threatened, many octopuses release a cloud of dark ink from a sac near the funnel. The ink contains melanin and mucus, and it can temporarily disorient a predator's vision or sense of smell. Octopuses often jet away right after releasing it. Some species also rely on decoys or sudden bursts of speed, and the ink's effectiveness depends on the species, the current, and the predator's senses.

Octopuses can regenerate lost arms. If an arm is torn off by a predator or injured in a struggle, the animal can grow a replacement over several months. The new arm may not be a perfect copy, but it restores the ability to hunt, crawl, and feel. Regeneration relies on specialized cells near the wound that rebuild muscle, nerve, and sucker tissue, although each loss costs the animal energy and time.

Most octopuses live only one to two years, and many species live less than a year. This short life is closely tied to reproduction. Females typically lay thousands of eggs and guard them until they hatch, often stopping to eat and weakening dramatically during that period. The mother dies soon after hatching, and many males die shortly after mating, so reproduction often marks the end of an individual's life.

The mimic octopus, found in Indo-Pacific waters, imitates other animals to avoid predators. It can impersonate venomous lionfish, flatfish, and sea snakes by changing its body shape, arm posture, and swimming style. Researchers believe it chooses which model to copy based on the threat it faces. Documented observations in the wild show how flexible octopus behavior can be when coloration, posture, and movement are combined.

Octopuses can solve problems and learn by observation. In laboratory tests they have opened jars to reach food, navigated mazes, and distinguished between individual humans. Some individuals in aquariums have been seen unscrewing bottle caps or removing lids. These behaviors suggest a level of cognitive flexibility that is unusual among invertebrates, although scientists still debate how to compare them with vertebrate intelligence.

Each sucker on an octopus arm contains chemoreceptors that can taste the surfaces it touches. This lets the animal tell whether an object is food before it picks it up. Each arm samples its surroundings independently, which helps explain why octopuses search crevices so effectively. The suckers also grip strongly by using muscles to create negative pressure, so the arms serve as both sensory organs and manipulators.

Octopuses sleep, and researchers have recorded alternating active and quiet states that resemble sleep cycles in other animals. During rest they often show changes in skin color and body posture, and some species appear to enter deeper states of inactivity. Scientists have also documented rapid color flashes during sleep, which may reflect internal processing, though this is not yet confirmed. Sleep research in octopuses remains limited, so its function is not fully understood.

More than 300 octopus species have been described, living in nearly every ocean from shallow tide pools to the deep sea. The Giant Pacific octopus, found along the North Pacific coast, can reach arm spans of more than 20 feet, while the star-sucker pygmy octopus is only about an inch long. This diversity reflects differences in habitat, diet, and body plan. Dumbo octopuses, named for their ear-like fins, live at great depths.

Octopuses belong to the cephalopod group, which also includes squid, cuttlefish, and nautiluses. Cephalopods diverged from other molluscs hundreds of millions of years ago. Many lineages lost their external shells over time, and octopuses have only tiny internal remnants or none at all. This soft, flexible body lets them squeeze through narrow openings, and it is one reason octopuses have colonized such varied environments.
